title: How caries happens: the Stephan curve
blurb: Sugar, plaque bacteria and acid: how enamel dissolves, why pH 5.5 matters and why how often you eat sugar counts more than how much.
question: A patient has three new cavities. She says she doesn't eat many sweets, but she sips a sugary coffee from mid-morning to mid-afternoon at her desk. The dentist asks you to explain to her why this habit is so damaging. What will you tell her?

teach.body: Dental caries (decay) is the breakdown of enamel and dentine by acid. The acid is made by plaque bacteria when they ferment sugars from our diet. Four things must come together: a tooth surface, plaque bacteria, fermentable sugar, and time. Remove any one and decay can't happen. That's why prevention targets all four: brushing removes plaque, fluoride strengthens the tooth, diet advice cuts sugar, and keeping sugar to mealtimes limits the time teeth spend under attack.

steps.label: Sugar eaten
steps.sub: Free sugars such as sucrose, glucose and fructose

steps.label: Bacteria ferment it
steps.sub: Streptococcus mutans and lactobacilli in plaque

steps.label: Acid produced
steps.sub: Mainly lactic acid, held against the tooth by plaque

steps.label: Demineralisation
steps.sub: Calcium and phosphate dissolve out of the enamel

teach.caption: Streptococcus mutans is linked with starting decay in enamel. Lactobacilli thrive in acid and are linked with decay progressing into dentine.

teach.body: If you measure plaque pH after a sugary snack, it drops within minutes, from a resting level near neutral to well below 5.5. While it stays below 5.5, enamel loses mineral. Saliva then gradually neutralises the acid and the pH climbs back. Recovery commonly takes from about 20 minutes to an hour. This dip-and-recover graph is called the Stephan curve. Every time sugar goes in, the curve starts again.

teach.caption: The shaded part under the line is the time enamel is demineralising. Above 5.5, saliva and fluoride can put mineral back.
Three acid attacks a day, with long gaps for saliva to repair the enamel.
The same sugar spread out: ten acid attacks and almost no recovery time. Demineralisation wins, and cavities form.

Saliva neutralises acid (mainly with bicarbonate), clears sugar and supplies calcium and phosphate. Fluoride speeds repair and makes enamel more acid-resistant. Decay happens when attacks outweigh repair.

head: Factor
Raises risk
Lowers risk
teach.caption: Fluoride toothpaste strengths follow Delivering Better Oral Health (4th edn) for adults and children aged 7 and over.

teach.text: Frequency matters more than amount. The same sugar eaten in one sitting causes one acid attack; nibbled or sipped over the afternoon it causes many. In exam questions about snacking, sipping or grazing, the answer is almost always about the NUMBER of sugar intakes.

items: Caries needs a tooth, plaque bacteria, fermentable sugar and time.
Bacteria (Streptococcus mutans, lactobacilli) ferment sugar into acid, mainly lactic acid.
Enamel demineralises below the critical pH of 5.5.
The Stephan curve: pH drops within minutes, then takes roughly 20–60 minutes to recover.
Each sugar intake is a new acid attack, so frequency matters more than amount.
Saliva and fluoride drive remineralisation once pH rises above 5.5.

summary: You can now explain how plaque bacteria turn sugar into acid, why enamel dissolves below pH 5.5, what the Stephan curve shows, how saliva and fluoride repair early damage, and why frequent sugar intake is more harmful than the same amount at mealtimes.

A.q: Below which plaque pH does enamel generally start to demineralise?
A.why: pH 5.5 is the critical pH for enamel. Below it, calcium and phosphate dissolve out of the hydroxyapatite.

whyNot.0: Enamel is already dissolving well before plaque reaches pH 4.5.
whyNot.2: pH 6.5 is close to resting plaque pH, when remineralisation can happen.
whyNot.3: pH 7.5 is slightly alkaline, which is safe for enamel.

A.q: Two patients eat the same amount of sugar daily. One has it with meals; the other sips sugary tea all day. Why is the second patient at higher caries risk?
options: Sugar in drinks soaks into enamel
Tea stains soften the enamel surface
Hot drinks reduce the flow of saliva
Each sip starts a new acid attack
A.why: Every sugar intake restarts the Stephan curve, so frequent sipping keeps plaque pH below 5.5 for much of the day.

whyNot.0: Sugar doesn't soak into enamel; bacteria turn it into acid in plaque.
whyNot.1: Tea staining is cosmetic and doesn't soften enamel.
whyNot.2: Hot drinks don't meaningfully reduce saliva; the problem is repeated acid attacks.

A.q: Which bacterium is most closely linked with starting caries in enamel?
A.why: Streptococcus mutans ferments sugar into acid and helps plaque stick to the tooth, so it is linked with starting enamel decay.

whyNot.1: Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with periodontitis, not caries.
whyNot.2: Staphylococcus aureus causes skin and wound infections, not dental caries.
whyNot.3: Candida albicans is a fungus that causes oral thrush.

B.q: A patient asks how the bacteria in plaque actually damage teeth. What is the main mechanism?
options: They release toxins that inflame enamel
They wear enamel away by friction
B.why: Plaque bacteria ferment dietary sugars into acid, which dissolves mineral out of enamel and dentine.

whyNot.0: Bacterial toxins inflame the gums; enamel has no living tissue to inflame.
whyNot.1: Friction is a cause of tooth wear (abrasion), not caries.
whyNot.3: Acid, not enzymes, is what dissolves enamel mineral in caries.

B.q: On a Stephan curve, what happens to plaque pH in the first few minutes after a sugary drink?
options: It rises sharply, then slowly falls
It falls quickly below the critical level
It stays level for about an hour
It falls slowly over several hours
B.why: Bacteria start making acid almost at once, so plaque pH falls within minutes to below 5.5.

whyNot.0: The curve shows a fall first, then a slow recovery: the opposite of this.
whyNot.2: pH changes within minutes of sugar; it doesn't stay level.
whyNot.3: The drop is rapid; it is the recovery that is slow.

B.q: Which of these is NOT a way saliva protects teeth against caries?
B.why: Saliva forms the pellicle rather than dissolving it. Its protective roles are buffering, clearing sugars and supplying minerals for repair.

whyNot.0: Buffering (mainly by bicarbonate) is a key way saliva raises pH after an acid attack.
whyNot.1: Saliva washes sugars away, shortening the acid attack.
whyNot.2: Calcium and phosphate in saliva are needed for remineralisation.

C.q: A patient taking several medicines complains of a constantly dry mouth. Why does this raise their caries risk?
options: Less saliva to buffer and repair
A dry mouth makes calculus form
C.why: With less saliva, acid is neutralised more slowly and there is less calcium and phosphate to remineralise enamel.

whyNot.0: Enamel doesn't absorb sugar; bacteria convert sugar into acid.
whyNot.1: The problem is reduced saliva, not loss of protective bacteria.
whyNot.3: Calculus is not the reason dry mouth raises caries risk.

C.q: Which dietary advice best reduces the number of acid attacks a patient's teeth suffer?
options: Brush straight after every sweet snack
Rinse with water before eating sweets
Choose fruit juice over fizzy drinks
C.why: Keeping sugar to mealtimes cuts the number of acid attacks and leaves time for saliva to repair enamel.

whyNot.0: Brushing doesn't stop the acid attack already started, and frequent snacking still causes repeated drops.
whyNot.1: Rinsing beforehand does nothing to stop bacteria turning the sugar into acid.
whyNot.2: Fruit juice is high in free sugars and is acidic too.

C.q: Put these in order: (1) demineralisation, (2) acid produced, (3) sugar eaten, (4) bacteria ferment sugar.
C.why: Sugar is eaten, plaque bacteria ferment it, acid is produced, and enamel demineralises once pH falls below 5.5.

whyNot.0: Bacteria can't ferment sugar before it is eaten.
whyNot.2: Acid is the product of fermentation, so it can't come first.
whyNot.3: Acid can't be produced before sugar is eaten and fermented.

reteach.title: Your teeth as a bank account
reteach.question: Imagine each tooth has a mineral bank account. Some things take mineral out; others pay it back in. When does the account go overdrawn?

blocks.body: Every time sugar goes into the mouth, plaque bacteria make acid and the tooth makes a withdrawal: calcium and phosphate leave the enamel. Between snacks, saliva pays mineral back in, and fluoride makes the deposit stronger. One withdrawal at each meal is easily repaid. But a withdrawal every half hour, with no time to pay back, sends the account overdrawn: that's a cavity.

blocks.h: Which side of 5.5 is the plaque?

rows.label: Sipping a sugary drink all afternoon

explain.body: Caries needs a tooth, plaque bacteria, fermentable sugar and time together. Bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans and lactobacilli ferment the sugar into acid, which dissolves enamel.

test.q: Which of these is NOT needed for caries to develop?
test.why: Caries needs a tooth, plaque bacteria, sugar and time. Calculus is linked with gum disease, not required for decay.

whyNot.0: Without sugar, bacteria have nothing to ferment into acid.
whyNot.1: Bacteria make the acid, so they are essential.
whyNot.2: There must be a tooth surface for acid to dissolve.

explain.body: The curve plots plaque pH against time after sugar. It drops within minutes, dips below the critical pH of 5.5 (demineralisation), then slowly recovers as saliva neutralises the acid.

test.q: On a Stephan curve, what does the line drawn at pH 5.5 represent?
options: The lowest pH plaque can reach
test.why: pH 5.5 is the critical pH: below it enamel demineralises, above it remineralisation can happen.

whyNot.1: Resting saliva is close to neutral, around pH 7.
whyNot.2: Toothpaste pH is not what the curve shows.
whyNot.3: Plaque pH can fall below 5.5; the line marks the danger level, not the floor.

explain.body: Each sugar intake restarts the curve. Grazing or sipping keeps plaque acidic for hours, so enamel never gets the chance to repair. Advise keeping sugary foods and drinks to mealtimes.

items.label: acid attacks: sugar with meals only
acid attacks: sipping and snacking all day

test.q: A teenager sips an energy drink containing sugar over three hours. What is the main problem for his teeth?
options: The sugar soaks into the enamel
Plaque pH stays low for hours
test.why: Sipping restarts the acid attack again and again, so plaque pH stays below 5.5 for long periods.

whyNot.0: Caffeine is not what causes decay.
whyNot.2: Sugar is turned into acid by bacteria; it doesn't soak into enamel.

explain.body: Once pH rises above 5.5, saliva redeposits calcium and phosphate into the enamel. Fluoride speeds this up and forms a more acid-resistant surface. Early lesions can be reversed if repair outweighs attack.

test.q: What allows an early enamel lesion to remineralise?
options: Saliva and fluoride after pH recovers
test.why: Once pH is above 5.5, saliva supplies calcium and phosphate, and fluoride helps them back into the enamel.

whyNot.0: Below 5.5 enamel loses mineral rather than regaining it.
whyNot.1: More sugar means more acid attacks.
whyNot.3: Scaling treats gum disease and doesn't remineralise enamel.
